title: Can observations pick an arrow?
hook: Two arrow patterns can fit the same observations. What remains unresolved?

knows: arithmetic means, rates and simple plotted values
doesNotKnow: A → B → C and A ← B ← C produce identical observational data.

misconception: Treating same data, different graphs as valid without checking the stated model, denominators or causal assumptions.
objective: A → B → C and A ← B ← C produce identical observational data.
keyState: Both finite cases completed; their computed summaries retained.

claims.text: Fair B independently flips into A and C with 10% error each. A←B→C and a fitted A→B→C factorization reproduce the same joint distribution. Can those observations alone pick the causal direction?
claims.source: src/demos/probability/p100-same-data-different-graphs/spec.ts; exact finite illustration specified in manager numericCase: Construct three correlated binary variables by choosing common B fair, independent10%bit flips for A,C. A←B→C and statistically factorized A→B→C generate same joint table; observational arrows not identified without assumptions/interventions. Builder show joint counts, not invented causal certainty.

claims.text: Arrows express causal assumptions beyond a distributional fit. These graphs can imply different interventions even when passive observations agree. Additional temporal, experimental or domain information is needed to distinguish their causal interpretations.

claims.text: Two causal graphs imply exactly the same observational distribution. What can separate their intervention predictions? Observationally equivalent models need information that breaks the equivalence, such as an appropriate intervention.
